$comment: Single source of truth. scripts/build.sh reads this to materialize build/ from upstream/. 'frontmatter' entries are the ONLY deviations from upstream; every one carries a 'reason'.

compound-engineering.note: Installed unmodified from the upstream marketplace at user scope. CE is the default lifecycle owner; its own descriptions are already mutually disambiguated, and its skills depend on plugin-level assets under src/. No deviations.

frontmatter.description: Deep root-cause diagnosis for a bug that ordinary debugging has already failed to explain. Use when the user asks for the root cause of a hard or recurring bug, says earlier fixes or hypotheses did not hold, or reports an unexplained race, flake, or performance regression that needs a measured bisect. Also use when the active debugging workflow escalates an inconclusive hypothesis loop. Not the first responder for an ordinary failing test, stack trace, or broken behaviour.

diagnosing-bugs.reason: Upstream trigger ('Use when the user says "diagnose"/"debug this", or reports something broken/throwing/failing/slow') is a direct owner-level collision with ce-debug. Rewritten as an escalation trigger: prior-attempt evidence or explicit root-cause request, plus delegation from the active debugger.

frontmatter.description: Second-opinion review of changes since a fixed point, split across a Standards axis and a Spec axis run as parallel sub-agents. Manual invocation only.

code-review.reason: Upstream trigger ('when the user wants to review a branch, a PR, work-in-progress changes') is an owner-level collision with ce-code-review. Demoted to MANUAL so a generic review request can never reach two reviewers; still available as /code-review for an explicit second opinion.

frontmatter.description: Interview the user round by round to stress-test a plan, design, or decision they have already formed, mapping it as a design tree and settling one frontier of questions per round. Use when the user explicitly asks to be grilled, interrogated, or challenged on their reasoning, or when the grill-me entry point delegates here. A questioning technique applied to an existing idea; it does not own brainstorming, scoping what to build, or product framing, and it writes no plan artifact.

grilling.reason: Upstream trigger ('Use when the user wants to stress-test their thinking') is a near-owner-level collision with ce-brainstorm, which owns requirements and product framing. Narrowed to an explicit grill request plus delegation from grill-me, with an explicit non-ownership clause, following the tdd pattern. Left model-invocable on purpose: grill-me's body calls this skill by name, and disable-model-invocation would withhold it from the skill listing and break that delegation.

grill-me.reason: User-facing entry point for grilling. Installed unmodified: upstream already ships disable-model-invocation: true, so it cannot compete with ce-brainstorm for any routing decision and needs no override. Carried as /grill-me for a deliberate stress-test of a plan the user already has.

frontmatter.description: Test-first methodology: drive a change through red-green-refactor, one failing test at a time. Use when the user asks to work test-first, says TDD or red-green-refactor, or wants the change proven by integration tests before the code lands. Also use when the active implementation workflow is told to build the change from tests. A methodology applied inside implementation; it does not own the implementation workflow.

tdd.reason: Added the delegation trigger and an explicit non-ownership boundary so tdd augments ce-work rather than competing with it for the implementation phase.

frontmatter.description: Settle what the project's nouns mean and write the decision down. Use when the user asks whether two or more terms name the same concept, wants the ubiquitous language or glossary sharpened, questions a name that has drifted, or is writing or editing a CONTEXT.md or an ADR. Not for module boundaries or interface shape, and not a general planning step.

domain-modeling.reason: Upstream description is short and its 'discussing codebase terminology' clause is vague enough to catch general planning. Sharpened to the concrete trigger (are these the same concept? / CONTEXT.md / ADR) and given a negative boundary against codebase-design.

frontmatter.description: Deep-module vocabulary for interface design: module depth, seams, information hiding, and where a boundary belongs. Use when the user asks where to split a module, how deep an interface should be, how to make code more testable or navigable, or when the active planning or implementation workflow needs that vocabulary to justify a boundary. Not for naming or domain concepts, and not a substitute for the plan itself.

codebase-design.reason: Added the delegation trigger and negative boundaries against domain-modeling and ce-plan so it augments rather than owns the planning phase.

setup-matt-pocock-skills.reason: Unmodified — already disable-model-invocation upstream. Included because code-review's Spec axis reads docs/agents/issue-tracker.md, which only this skill writes.

frontmatter.description: Write documents an agent consumes: a SKILL.md, an AGENTS.md or CLAUDE.md, a doc reached by a pointer. Covers context pointers and how their wording decides what fires, the split between context load and cognitive load, progressive disclosure, and completion criteria that stop a step ending early. Use when creating or editing a skill, when editing AGENTS.md or CLAUDE.md, or when an agent-facing doc has sprawled. Not for prose written for people.

writing-for-agents.reason: Upstream description is one line, 'Writing documents for agents. Use when creating or editing skills, or modifying AGENTS.md or CLAUDE.md.' Accurate but thin, and it names no branch beyond the file types, so it competes weakly against unslop and technical-writing on any doc task. Expanded to name what the skill actually decides, and given a negative boundary against human-facing prose. Added after the coverage matrix showed no installed skill owned agent-facing documents, which is most of the work in the four-repo documentation pass.

excluded.implement, to-spec, to-tickets, wayfinde: Owner-level or near-owner-level competitors to the Compound lifecycle (planning, requirements, implementation, handoff, learning), or duplicates of a Compound skill (ce-prototype, ce-handoff, ce-explain, ce-pov). Excluded rather than demoted, to keep the skill listing small. (writing-for-agents has since been installed: it owns agent-facing documents, a domain nothing else covered. grilling and grill-me have since been installed: grilling narrowed to an explicit grill request with a non-ownership clause, grill-me unmodified because it is already manual-only. ce-brainstorm keeps sole ownership of requirements.)
excluded.resolving-merge-conflicts, wizard, git-g: Useful but outside the four lifecycle domains this stack curates; omitted to protect the context budget. Add with scripts/build.sh if wanted.

frontmatter.description: Vercel Engineering's rules for writing React and Next.js: request waterfalls, bundle size, server rendering, data fetching, and re-render cost. Consult when writing or changing a React component, hook, form, or data fetch, including feature requests that describe the interface without naming the framework. Also use when explaining why React code is slow. Its Next.js App Router, RSC, server-action and next/dynamic rules apply only inside a Next.js project and are skipped elsewhere. An advisory overlay for the workflow already running; it does not own implementation and is not a code-review or PR-review workflow.

react-best-practices.reason: Upstream said 'used when writing, reviewing, or refactoring React/Next.js code'. The 'reviewing' verb made it a candidate owner for code review, so it was removed. Two eval rounds then chased a reliability problem. The first narrowing only fired when a prompt named React or Next: 'add a settings page to this Next.js application' fired 3/3, 'build me an export-to-CSV button on the settings page' 0/2. Widening to cover unnamed-framework UI work lifted that to 1/2, still unreliable. The fix was the opening clause: leading with 'performance rules' let the model judge the skill irrelevant to a plain feature build, so it now leads with 'rules for writing React and Next.js' and says consult by default. Third pass, 2026-08-24: 'Consult by default on any React or Next.js work' was demoted to 'Consult when'. No repo in this environment uses Next.js, so the default-consult claim pulled roughly 3,800 lines of App Router, RSC and server-action guidance into context on work where none of its ten CRITICAL rules apply. The Next-only material is now explicitly fenced rather than presented as the priority. React itself is still in use, so the skill stays PASSIVE.

frontmatter.description: React component API design: compound components, children over render props, explicit variants instead of boolean prop proliferation, context boundaries, and the React 19 ref change. Use when designing or refactoring the public shape of a reusable component — too many boolean props, a component library API, or a prop interface that has stopped scaling. A design overlay for component interfaces, not a general React performance or implementation workflow.

composition-patterns.reason: Upstream 'component architecture' clause overlapped both react-best-practices and codebase-design. Narrowed to the public shape of a component's props, with a negative boundary against the performance overlay.

frontmatter.description: Audit UI code against the Web Interface Guidelines — accessibility, focus states, forms, motion, typography, images, touch targets, theming, and i18n. Use when the user explicitly asks for a UI, UX, design, or accessibility review, or when the active review workflow flags an interface surface that needs one. Not the default reviewer for a general code or PR review, and not a React performance pass.

web-design-guidelines.reason: Upstream 'check my site against best practices' is broad enough to catch a generic review request. Replaced with an explicit-request-or-delegation trigger and a negative boundary against general review.

frontmatter.description: Implement animations with React's View Transition API — <ViewTransition>, addTransitionType, and CSS view-transition pseudo-elements. Use for page or route transition animations, shared-element transitions, enter/exit or list-reorder animation, or directional back/forward navigation animation in React and Next.js, and whenever startViewTransition or ViewTransition is mentioned. React only — it does not apply to Astro's native ClientRouter, transition:name or transition:persist, which are a different API that this skill's class-keyed ::view-transition-old(.class) selectors never match.

react-view-transitions.reason: Trigger unchanged in substance; compressed from 92 to 58 words for the context budget. Second pass, 2026-08-24: kept rather than dropped, but fenced. The stack now serves an Astro repo that ships native view transitions, and there the skill is actively misleading — it proposes <ViewTransition> wrappers and a react@canary install for a feature already working, and its class-keyed pseudo-element recipes silently never match Astro's name-based groups. Removing it outright would have cost the one React repo in this environment a valid skill, so the trigger carries an explicit Astro exclusion instead.

frontmatter.description: Audit a deployed Vercel project for cost and performance: collect account metrics first, investigate only metric-backed candidates, produce ranked recommendations. Manual invocation only.

vercel-optimize.reason: Expensive and side-reaching — it pulls billing and analytics data from the connected Vercel account. Phase 3 puts that in MANUAL. Description trimmed accordingly since it is now slash-only.

excluded.deploy-to-vercel, vercel-cli-with-tokens: Deployment is already owned in this environment by the Vercel MCP server (mcp__vercel__deploy_to_vercel and friends), which is authenticated and account-aware. Installing these skills would put two owners on the deployment phase.
excluded.react-native-skills: No React Native or Expo work in this environment.
excluded.writing-guidelines: Vercel-house-voice prose review; no owner conflict, but nothing in this stack routes to it.

trailofbits.note: Forked into a local marketplace rather than installed from trailofbits/skills, because several of these plugins carry plugin-level agents, hooks, commands, and CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT-relative workflows that only survive a plugin install — and their routing metadata cannot be changed from outside the plugin. The fork is regenerated from upstream/ by scripts/build.sh; Claude's plugin cache is never edited.

frontmatter.description: Security-focused differential review of a diff, commit range, or pull request: threat-model the change, compute blast radius, and hunt for security regressions the change introduces. Use when the user explicitly asks for a security review of changes, or when the active review workflow finds the diff touches a security-sensitive surface — authentication, authorization, permissions, secrets, cryptography, payments or value transfer, untrusted input, deserialization, file upload, external calls, unsafe or native boundaries, dependency changes, or security configuration. Not for a general request to review a PR with no security signal.

differential-review.reason: Upstream ('Performs security-focused differential review of code changes (PRs, commits, diffs)') had no activation condition and no negative boundary, so a bare 'review this PR' could pull it in alongside ce-code-review. Rewritten with an explicit-request-or-delegation trigger, the enumerated security surfaces, and a negative boundary.

frontmatter.description: Run a Semgrep static-analysis scan over a codebase and merge the results to SARIF, with an explicit approval gate on the ruleset plan. Use when the user asks to run Semgrep, run a SAST or static-analysis scan, or scan the codebase for known vulnerability patterns. Not a general code review, not a debugging step, and not for reading a scan that already exists.

semgrep.reason: Upstream trigger included 'find bugs' and 'run a security audit', which collide with ce-debug and ce-code-review. Removed both phrases and added negative boundaries.

frontmatter.description: Scan a codebase with CodeQL interprocedural data-flow and taint tracking, building the database first. Manual invocation only.

codeql.reason: Expensive (builds a CodeQL database, minutes to hours) and its upstream trigger 'find vulnerabilities in this repo' is broad. Phase 3 puts expensive workflows in MANUAL. Semgrep remains the model-invocable static-analysis path.

sarif-parsing.reason: Unmodified — already narrow, with a negative boundary against the scanners.

supply-chain-risk-auditor.reason: Unmodified — sole owner of the supply-chain domain, trigger already specific. The router carries the rule that it runs directly rather than wrapped in the Compound feature lifecycle.

variant-analysis.domain: security review (spread of a known bug)

variant-analysis.reason: Unmodified — upstream already states the precondition (a bug in hand) and the negative boundary (not initial discovery).

fp-check.reason: Unmodified — upstream already bounds it to verifying a specific suspected finding, explicitly not hunting.

frontmatter.description: Find footguns in an API or configuration surface: error-prone signatures, unsafe defaults, and shapes that make misuse easy. Use when the user asks whether an API, config schema, or crypto wrapper is misuse-resistant or secure by default, or when a security review flags a dangerous default. Triggers: footgun, misuse-resistant, secure by default, pit of success. Not a general code review and not a vulnerability scan.

sharp-edges.reason: Upstream 'Use when reviewing API designs, configuration schemas' reads as a review trigger. Reframed as a question about misuse-resistance, with a negative boundary against general review.

agentic-actions-auditor.reason: Unmodified — trigger is already confined to workflow files that invoke AI agents.

frontmatter.description: Read an unfamiliar codebase function by function before hunting for bugs in it, recording what each one assumes, guarantees, and depends on. Manual invocation only.

audit-context-building.reason: A whole-codebase pass that is expensive by design, and 'before any vulnerability-hunting pass' would let it front-run every security escalation. MANUAL, so it starts a deliberate audit rather than joining an ordinary one.

insecure-defaults.note: Command-only plugin — ships /insecure-defaults:audit with no SKILL.md, so it has no model-invocable surface and needs no deviation.

frontmatter.description: Modern Python project tooling — uv for environments and dependencies, ruff for lint and format, ty for type checking. Use whenever Python is being set up or run: a new project, a one-off or standalone script, adding or pinning a dependency, a requirements.txt or pyproject.toml edit, or a migration off pip, Poetry, mypy, or black. A tooling overlay; it does not own implementation or planning.

modern-python.reason: Added after profiling the environment: four Python repos, all on requirements.txt. The trigger gained an explicit non-ownership clause so it advises ce-work rather than competing with it. Originally excluded from this stack as out of scope — that call was made before the environment was profiled and was wrong. A first probe then showed the narrowed trigger never fired on 'write a standalone script' (0/2) — the model read the task as too small to need tooling advice. The trigger now names the concrete moments Python tooling is chosen, rather than the abstract activity.

modern-python.note: The plugin's hooks/ directory is excluded from the fork. Upstream ships a SessionStart hook that prepends PATH shims intercepting python, pip, pipx and uv in every session. The guidance is worth having; a global PATH interception that silently activates the moment uv appears on the machine is not something to install by side effect. Restore it by removing excludePaths and rebuilding.

excluded.second-opinion: Runs an external LLM review of a diff — a third owner in the code-review domain alongside ce-code-review and the Pocock second opinion. Excluded rather than demoted.
excluded.gh-cli, git-cleanup, github-triage: Compound owns the git/PR/CI lifecycle. gh-cli in particular intercepts ordinary GitHub fetches and would fire constantly.
excluded.property-based-testing, mutation-testing: Would put a third voice in the testing domain alongside Compound and the Pocock TDD methodology. Genuinely useful — add deliberately if the testing strategy calls for them.
excluded.c-review, rust-review, modern-cpp, writi: Language or tooling surfaces absent from this environment.
excluded.building-secure-contracts, entry-point-a: Smart-contract and binary-analysis specialisms; no blockchain or native work here. trailmark also needs an external binary.
excluded.devcontainer-setup, open-sourcing, goal-: Out of scope for a general engineering lifecycle, or duplicative of skills already installed.

cursor.note: A fifth source, deliberately outside the engineering stack. cursor/plugins is MIT with a LICENSE per plugin; the unslop skill lives under pstack, (c) 2026 Lauren Tan.

frontmatter.description: Cut AI tells from prose: puffery, formulaic transitions, vague attribution, em-dash pileups, and the rhythms that read as machine-written. Use when asked to unslop, de-slop, humanise, or clean up drafted writing, when prose is said to sound like ChatGPT or read as robotic, and when drafting or revising a README, doc, or announcement meant for people to read. Not for code, commit messages, or code comments.

unslop.reason: Upstream description is 'Cut AI tells from any writing. Must always apply.' — an unconditional trigger with no boundary, which in an engineering session would fire on commit messages, code comments, and every incidental piece of text. Narrowed to human-facing prose, with the negative boundary against code, and the concrete trigger words kept.

cli-for-agents.reason: Unmodified. Its trigger is already confined to building or reviewing a CLI, a domain no other skill in the stack claims.

frontmatter.description: Reconstruct why a decision was made, from the evidence rather than from the code as it stands: source control, issue tracker, long-form docs, chat, incident history. Use for "why does X work this way", "why did we pick Y", design rationale, a regression whose origin matters, a postmortem, or a threshold nobody can justify. Not for how something works today, and not a planning or review step.

why.reason: Upstream trigger listed the phrasings but not the boundary, leaving it adjacent to ce-explain (which teaches how something works) and ce-pov (which gives a verdict). Added the explicit contrast so it takes only the archaeology question.

technical-writing.reason: Unmodified, including its upstream disable-model-invocation. A documentation standard rather than an engineering skill: Diataxis structure, Google developer style, STE instruction rules, Global English syntax. Manual by design, so it costs nothing in the skill listing and runs only when typed. Paired with unslop, which removes AI tells, while this one decides what kind of document is being written and how its sentences address the reader.

excluded.review-and-ship, thermo-nuclear-code-qua: Compound owns review, CI, and the shipping tail. Several of these are good skills; none can run without putting a second owner on a phase Compound already holds.
excluded.teach, continual-learning, recall, refle: Duplicates of ce-explain, ce-compound, and ce-handoff.
excluded.tdd (pstack), architect, how, figure-it-: Overlap the Pocock methodology layer and ce-plan.
excluded.principle-* (21 skills): A MANUAL principle set. Free contextually, but most of it restates what Compound and the Pocock layer already encode, and 21 slash commands is its own kind of clutter.
excluded.arena, swarm, orchestrate, ralph-loop, r: Multi-agent orchestration, which this host provides natively through Workflow and Agent.
excluded.typescript-best-practices: A real gap, but its trigger is 'any .ts or .tsx file' — it would fire on every TypeScript touch. Worth revisiting with a narrowed description.
excluded.control-ui, control-cli, create-verifica: Overlap the project's own verify-site skill and ToB fp-check.
excluded.benny automations, setup-pstack, poteto-: Personal-workflow and automation scaffolding for another person's setup.

hashicorp.note: Three skills of sixteen. The plugin is not installed: twelve of its skills are for developing Terraform providers (new-terraform-provider, provider-resources, provider-docs, provider-framework-migration, provider-actions, provider-configuration, provider-ephemeral-resources, provider-test-patterns, run-acceptance-tests) or are tied to Azure and paid HCP products (azure-verified-modules, terraform-stacks, terraform-policy). MPL-2.0 is file-level weak copyleft: these three files stay MPL and are marked as such.

frontmatter.description: HashiCorp's official HCL style conventions — file layout, naming, argument order, variable and output structure, comments. Consult when writing or editing Terraform configuration. A conventions overlay; it does not own the implementation workflow.

terraform-style-guide.reason: Upstream said 'Use when writing, reviewing, or generating Terraform configurations'. The 'reviewing' verb made it a candidate for the code-review phase, the same problem react-best-practices had. Removed, and non-ownership stated.

frontmatter.description: Turn a monolithic Terraform configuration into reusable modules: what belongs in a module, its variable and output surface, and how to move resources without destroying them. Use when a flat pile of .tf files needs structure, when the same resources are being copied between environments, or when asked to modularise Terraform.

refactor-module.reason: Upstream description was a capability statement with no activation condition. Added the concrete triggers, including the state-move concern that makes this risky to do by hand.

terraform-test.reason: Unmodified — already specific to .tftest.hcl, run blocks, assertions, and mocked providers.

excluded.packer plugin: AMI and Azure image building. This environment builds Docker images.
excluded.the nine provider-development skills: For authors of Terraform providers, not consumers of them.
excluded.azure-verified-modules, terraform-stacks: Azure-specific, or tied to paid HCP products.
excluded.terraform-search-import: Bringing unmanaged cloud resources under Terraform. Borderline — worth adding if drift between the AWS console and infra/ turns up.

aws.note: Forked and trimmed rather than installed whole. The upstream plugin ships 21 skills and costs about 5,000 always-on tokens, roughly 250 per skill, and more than half of them cover services absent from this environment (Swift SDK, Keyspaces, Neptune, Timestream, DocumentDB, CDK, CloudFormation, CodePipeline). Nine are kept. The plugin's MCP server, hooks, and manifests are preserved, which is why this is a plugin fork and not a set of vendored skills.

frontmatter.description: AWS operations from Python: service clients and resources, sessions and credentials, ClientError handling, paginators and waiters, S3 uploads, downloads and presigned URLs, DynamoDB table operations, and boto3 or botocore client configuration. Use for any AWS service call written in a Python codebase, including requests that name the service and the operation without naming Python, boto3, or botocore. Use whenever code imports boto3 or botocore, or the user asks about AWS from Python.

aws-sdk-python-usage.reason: Every clause of the upstream trigger was conditioned on the prompt naming Python, boto3, or botocore: 'when writing Python code that uses AWS services via boto3', 'whenever Python code imports boto3', 'when the user asks about AWS operations in Python'. In a mixed repo the model cannot confirm that without opening files, so 'add a function that uploads the rendered video to S3 and returns a presigned URL' fired it 1/3 even though the upstream text lists presigned URLs by name. The trigger now keys on the AWS operation in a Python codebase, the same fix react-best-practices needed.

aws-core.pluginDescription: AWS services used in this environment: boto3 and JS v3 SDK usage, Amazon Bedrock, Secrets Manager, S3 storage, IAM, SQS and EventBridge messaging, CloudWatch and X-Ray observability, and cost management.
aws-core.pluginDescriptionReason: The upstream blurb advertises CDK, CloudFormation, Aurora, DynamoDB, DocumentDB, Keyspaces, Neptune, Timestream and the Swift SDK. None of those skills survive the trim, so the manifest would have described capabilities the fork does not ship.

excluded.launch-with-aws: An owner-shaped migration workflow ('analysis through migration to deployment') that would compete with ce-work and with the Vercel MCP for the deployment phase. It never fired in the routing eval, but removing it removes the risk.
excluded.aws-cdk, aws-cloudformation, aws-deploym: This environment's IaC is Terraform, and its CI is GitHub Actions, not CodePipeline.
excluded.aws-database: Routes across Aurora, DynamoDB, DocumentDB, Keyspaces, Neptune and Timestream. The databases here are plain PostgreSQL reached through SQLAlchemy.
excluded.aws-sdk-swift-usage, aws-ai-ml, aws-bloc: No Swift, SageMaker, AWS Blocks, EC2, ECS or Lambda surface in this environment. aws-containers is the likeliest of these to be wanted back once the Docker services land on ECS.

jakubkrehel.note: Two of eleven. Both are values-layer skills: they carry the concrete numbers (leading ratios, measure caps, tracking by size, breakpoint derivation) that no installed skill supplies. Both close with a Block/Approve verdict, which is a review-phase output; since build.py rewrites frontmatter only and never bodies, that verdict is disclaimed in each description instead of removed.

frontmatter.description: Web typography values: woff2 delivery, variable-font axes through CSS properties rather than raw feature tags, type-scale construction, line-height by role, letter-spacing by size, measure caps, text-wrap, tabular numbers, truncation, and the iOS 16px input rule. Use when setting or correcting type values in CSS — a font-size that bypasses the scale, a leading that will not scale, an uncapped measure, a font loading the wrong axis. Supplies values to the workflow already running: it does not own review, and its closing Block/Approve verdict does not apply. Where a repo ships its own design spec, that spec wins on typeface, casing and punctuation.

better-typography.reason: Three deviations, all in the description. (1) Upstream triggers on a ~20-keyword list ('typography, font loading, woff2, variable fonts, ... drop cap') broad enough to co-fire with frontend-design on any design task; narrowed to the act of setting or correcting a type value. (2) Upstream ends 'End with Block when any HIGH remains, Approve otherwise' — an owner-level review verdict that collides with ce-code-review. Bodies are never edited here (build.py apply_overrides touches frontmatter only), so the description disclaims it. (3) Its handoffs to sibling skills better-accessibility, better-colors, better-ui and better-writing are dangling — none are installed. Rather than name substitutes in the description, the spec-wins clause covers the one case that actually bites: upstream mandates curly quotes and natural-case copy, which contradicts unslop rules 17/19 and the house style in a consuming repo's own design doc.

frontmatter.description: Layout structure and adaptivity: container queries over media queries, logical properties over physical ones, breakpoints derived from where content stops fitting rather than from device presets, full-bleed content with inset controls, safe-area insets, and grouping by space before lines. Use when structuring or reflowing a page or component, deciding what collapses at small sizes, or replacing a hand-rolled pixel breakpoint. A mechanics overlay for the workflow already running: it does not own review, and its closing Block/Approve verdict does not apply. Hit areas and focus belong to web-design-guidelines.

better-layout.reason: Same two structural deviations as better-typography: the keyword trigger list is narrowed to the act of structuring or reflowing, and the Block/Approve verdict is disclaimed because it is an owner-level review output. Its hit-area handoff is redirected to web-design-guidelines, which is installed, rather than to the uninstalled better-accessibility. Its RTL and pseudo-localization material is inert in a single-locale environment and is left in place rather than trimmed — bodies are not edited, and an unused section costs only context.

excluded.better-accessibility, better-colors: web-design-guidelines already owns accessibility and contrast review, and axe runs inside the consuming repo's own verify gate. Installing these puts a second owner on that phase.
excluded.better-ui, better-interface, explain-int: Owner-level competitors. interface-review is a review workflow (ce-code-review), explain-interface is a teaching artifact (ce-explain), and better-ui/better-interface duplicate frontend-design's remit on new surfaces.
excluded.better-writing: unslop owns prose that ships; technical-writing owns the docs.
excluded.break, variant: Adversarial stress-testing and variant generation — useful, but outside the domains this stack curates, and break overlaps the security plugins already installed.

emilkowalski.note: One of twelve. The only motion guidance in the stack carrying real numbers — per-element duration budgets, a frequency table, interruptibility mechanics. The eleven siblings are construction-side or platform-specific and would collide with ce-work.

frontmatter.description: Audit a whole surface's motion and return prioritized findings with exact target values: easing and duration budgets, purpose-and-frequency gating, interruptibility, transform-origin, reduced-motion, and token cohesion. Read-only on source. Manual invocation only; it hands findings to the planning owner. Its execute variant is not used here — implementation, worktrees and diff verdicts belong to the ce-* lifecycle. Where a repo ships a motion spec, that spec is the authority and these tables are the fallback.

improve-animations.reason: Demoted to MANUAL rather than narrowed. Two reasons, both matching how vercel-optimize was handled in Phase 3. First, expense: Phase 2 of the workflow fans out up to eight read-only subagents, and Phase 4 writes plan files into the consuming repo. Side-effecting and expensive workflows are never auto-selected. Second, trigger breadth: upstream fires on 'make this app feel better', which is a claim on any frontend request. The skill itself is well behaved — its Hard Rule 1 forbids touching source and its Hard Rule 4 is a prompt-injection defence — so the only real collision is the execute invocation variant, which dispatches an executor into a worktree and renders a verdict on the diff: ce-work, ce-worktree and ce-code-review at once. The description disclaims that variant. Demoting also neutralizes its dangling reference to review-animations, which is not installed. AUDIT.md and PLAN-TEMPLATE.md travel with it; SKILL.md alone is inert, since the values live in AUDIT.md.

excluded.animate: Construction-side — it writes the implementation, which is ce-work's phase. Its curve table is also a near-miss of tokens already shipping in the portfolio (--ease-out: cubic-bezier(0.23, 1, 0.32, 1) against a repo's 0.22, 1, 0.36, 1), and its Hard Rule 2 'never invent, come from the tables below' is worded more forcefully than its Hard Rule 3 'extend the codebase's tokens'. It would quietly fork the system it was brought in to protect.
excluded.review-animations: Owner-level collision with ce-code-review on the diff-review phase.

$local.$comment: Skills authored in this repo, built from src/ by scripts/build.py. Not vendored, so no pinned SHA — the git history here IS the provenance.
